RQ1: test descriptor drift as the "appearance hurts" mechanism — it doesn't

The stationary crossover left a hypothesis: appearance turns harmful when it is
confidently wrong, i.e. an object's descriptor drifts so its EMA gallery goes
stale and matches a look-alike neighbour. Model it and test it.

synthetic.py: add appearance_drift_std — each object's descriptor walks along a
fixed random direction, so emitted features are non-stationary. Gated on
drift_std>0 (drawn only when enabled) so the committed stationary crossover
reproduces bit-for-bit; off by default, existing scenes unchanged.

Result (w_app=0.8, 16 seeds): drift NEVER flips the sign. Across every
diversity level it makes ΔIDSW *more* negative and significant (e.g. identical
objects: −0.62 n.s. → −4.56 p<0.01 at drift 0.1). The reason is geometric —
independent random walks in high-dim space are near-orthogonal, so objects
*diverge* in appearance space and become MORE distinguishable, not confusable.

Refined RQ1 conclusion: two natural mechanisms (visual similarity, descriptor
drift) both fail to make appearance hurt — similarity is inert, drift helps.
In a cost-based ByteTrack with an EMA gallery appearance is robustly
non-harmful here; the DanceTrack "appearance hurts" regime needs *convergent*
confusion (objects converging in appearance, or a hard-committing association
policy), not mere similarity or non-stationarity.

the probe. PHASE3.md + README updated with the tested (not hypothesised)
conclusion. 2 new tests (drift off = stationary; drift on = non-stationary
descriptors). 269 tests pass, lint clean. No new deps; core still NumPy-only.

The plan doc described the four phases at a high level but gave nothing
executable for Phase 1. Adds the detail needed to start.

Settles the repo question with a reason that only became true at v0.2.0:
visiontrack-mot is on PyPI, so the sibling can depend on the NumPy reference
as a pinned versioned dependency rather than a path or submodule. The oracle
becomes an installable artifact, the dependency runs one way, and this repo
changes not at all.

Records the verified toolchain (clang 17 arm64, CMake 4.0.0, Eigen, pybind11
3.1.0 — nothing left to install), the exact port surface at ~1,438 LOC across
seven modules, and what is deliberately excluded: ONNX appearance inference
stays in Python behind a float-array boundary, GMC and the motion residual are
out, and no optimization happens in Phase 1 at all.

Replaces the vague "metrics match within tolerance" gate with a trajectory-level
one. Association is discrete, so a 1e-16 cost difference can flip an assignment
and cascade through every later frame while MOTA barely moves - metric parity
would pass a visibly wrong tracker. The gate is now identical (frame, track_id,
box) streams across all three cached MOT17-09 detector variants.

Names the tie-break trap explicitly, since it is the likeliest failure: the
transpose in linear_assignment and the scan order in _kuhn_munkres both decide
which of several equal-cost optima is returned, so both must be replicated
index-for-index rather than merely implemented correctly.

Sets the expectation that Phase 1 produces no speedup and may be slower than
vectorized NumPy - the deliverable is the harness that makes Phase 2 credible.

docs: record the Phase 2 and Phase 4 outcomes against the plan

Phases 2 (CPU optimization) and 4 (package + benchmark) are complete in the
sibling repo. This scores them against the plan's own predictions, the way the
Phase 1 outcome section did, and unparks the sibling in STATUS.md — which still
described it as "held pending a plan".

Phase 2's result is that the plan's optimization list was mostly illegal. The
governing rule, which the plan did not contain, is that an optimization is
legal only if every floating-point operation still happens in the same order,
on the same values, with the same rounding. Its corollary forecloses most of
the playbook: SIMD across independent problems is fine, SIMD within a reduction
reassociates a sum and is not. LAPJV was implemented correctly and bought
nothing measurable, because all nine of its disagreements with the Hungarian
solver on real data fall on pairs the gate discards anyway.

Phase 4 delivered all three items, and turned up the most transferable result
of the exercise: the parity harness had been under-reporting the port by ~21%.
It runs both trackers in one loop, which the gate requires, but NumPy's
allocations evict the C++ tracker's working set between calls — ~2us on a 9.5us
frame, versus 0.3% of a 700us NumPy frame. An instrument built to prove
agreement was biased when asked about speed, in the direction that understated
the result. Real figures: 55-74x on MOT17-09, 71-91x synthetic, with 100,765
observations compared bit-for-bit first.

Also records that parity survives an Eigen change (3.4.0 and 3.5.0, both zero
divergences), so the bit-exactness claim is not an artifact of one build host.

The plan's hardware caveat was right and still binds: Phase 3 needs a GPU this
machine does not have.

Record Phase 3's outcome and correct the plan's Metal recommendation

The plan offered Metal Performance Shaders as the local alternative to
CUDA. That advice does not apply to this codebase: Apple GPUs have no
float64, Metal has float and half and no double, and the tracker computes
in double throughout including the covariance Cholesky. The caveat section
now carries an inline correction rather than being quietly rewritten, and
the scoring table records it as a miss.

The plan also named the wrong kernels. It proposed offloading batched
predict and the IoU/cost matrix; Phase 2 measured predict at 0.4% of a
400-track frame, an Amdahl ceiling of 1.004x. The only GPU-shaped stage is
gating, which the plan never mentions, and which Phase 2 had already
localised to N*M independent 4x4 solves.

Phase 3 is therefore closed by measurement rather than blocked on
hardware. MOT17-09's median frame spends 0.85us in gating; measured
dispatch is 128-317us via torch MPS and the real-sequence row stays
unfavourable down to ~850ns. Where dispatch amortises, the ceiling is
1.33-1.82x. That retires the question a rented GPU would otherwise have
left open.
